plan: Ten new items aimed at harder reasoning after recent batches calibrated mostly easy. Every topic and choice set checked against the live bank (an 'Ultimately' transition was avoided because 208 keys it). circumscribed/vindicated WIC, banana monoculture sentence function, locust serotonin inference, bat light-color data (three-condition comparison, two columns), language-and-direction cross-text with a confound, Hubble/Webb contrast synthesis, 'Granted' concession, direct-question end mark after a colon, past counterfactual tense. Relabelled to the blind solvers' rating where it was lower: S038-02 medium→easy, S038-03 hard→easy, S038-04 hard→easy, S038-05 hard→easy, S038-06 hard→easy, S038-07 medium→easy, S038-09 medium→easy, S038-10 hard→medium.

passages.title: A limited committee
passages.text: The new oversight committee's authority is notably ______: it may review the city's budget and recommend changes, but it cannot approve, reject, or delay any spending on its own.

passages.title: An idea proved right
passages.text: When Alfred Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents had once been joined and had slowly drifted apart, most geologists rejected the idea because he could not explain what force moved them. Half a century later, maps of the ocean floor revealed new crust forming along mid-ocean ridges and spreading outward, providing the mechanism Wegener had lacked. His central claim was ______ by evidence he never lived to see.

passages.title: A fragile fruit
passages.text: Until the 1950s, most bananas sold in North America and Europe were of a single variety, the Gros Michel. Because commercial bananas are grown from cuttings rather than seeds, every Gros Michel plant was genetically almost identical to every other. When a soil fungus that causes Panama disease spread through plantations, no plants had natural resistance, and growers were forced to switch to a resistant variety, the Cavendish. Today the Cavendish dominates the export trade in the same way, and a new strain of the same fungus has begun to attack it.

passages.title: Crowded locusts
passages.text: Desert locusts usually live alone and avoid one another. When they are crowded together, however, they can switch within hours to a swarming form that seeks out other locusts and travels in huge groups. Researchers found that repeatedly touching the hind legs of solitary locusts triggered this switch and was accompanied by a sharp rise in serotonin, a chemical messenger in the nervous system. When locusts were given a drug that blocks serotonin's effects and then crowded together, they ______

passages.title: Bats and streetlights
passages.text:
Researchers counted bat passes per night near experimental streetlights of three colors, separately for bat species that avoid light and species that hunt insects attracted to light.
Light condition | Light-avoiding species | Light-tolerant species
No light | 40 | 50
White light | 10 | 90
Red light | 36 | 55
The researchers concluded that red light let light-avoiding bats remain nearly as active as they were in darkness, unlike white light.

passages.title: Language and direction (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, an Aboriginal Australian language, describe locations using cardinal directions ("the cup is north of the plate") rather than words like "left" and "right." In tests, they keep track of compass directions with remarkable accuracy, even indoors. Some researchers conclude that the language people speak shapes how they think about space.
Text 2
Critics point out that communities using cardinal-direction languages often also live in landscapes and follow daily routines that demand constant attention to direction. In studies that compared people who speak the same language but live in different environments, sense of direction tracked environment and habits about as closely as it tracked language.

passages.title: Two space telescopes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990.
• Hubble observes mainly visible and ultraviolet light.
• The James Webb Space Telescope was launched in 2021.
• Webb observes mainly infrared light, which can pass through clouds of dust that block visible light.
• Webb orbits about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth, much farther than Hubble.

passages.title: A demanding vaccine
passages.text: ______ the new vaccine must be kept at temperatures far below freezing, which makes it difficult to deliver to remote clinics. In trials, however, it prevented about 95 percent of cases, a level of protection that health officials say justifies the extra effort.

passages.title: An old question
passages.text: For centuries, naturalists were puzzled by a question that no one could answer with certainty: where do European eels go to spawn______ Not until the 1920s did researchers trace the youngest larvae to the Sargasso Sea.

passages.title: A near miss
passages.text: Astronomers estimate that if the comet ______ even slightly closer to the Sun during its 2020 pass, the heat would probably have broken it apart.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: but it cannot approve, reject, or delay any spending
candidates.explanation: The committee can only review and recommend, not act, so its authority is narrowly limited: "circumscribed."

A.rationale: The committee cannot approve or reject spending, so its authority is far from absolute.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests another body already does the same job.

D.rationale: The text says nothing about whether such a committee has existed before.

hints: What can and can't the committee do?
candidates.remember: The detail after the colon defines the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: providing the mechanism Wegener had lacked
candidates.explanation: A claim rejected at first and later supported by new evidence is "vindicated."

A.rationale: The ocean-floor evidence supported his claim rather than weakening it.

B.rationale: The evidence came after his claim and confirmed it; it did not foresee it.

C.rationale: The evidence made his claim clearer and more convincing, not harder to see.

hints: Did the later evidence help or hurt his claim?
candidates.remember: Track the shift from rejection to support.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the last sentence in the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It suggests that the vulnerability described in the earlier history may be repeating itself.
choices.B: It explains why growers in the 1950s chose the Cavendish to replace the Gros Michel.
choices.C: It offers a practical solution to the problem of growing bananas from cuttings.
choices.D: It shows that the Gros Michel has since recovered and returned to stores in large numbers.

candidates.evidence: in the same way, and a new strain of the same fungus has begun to attack it
candidates.explanation: The text explains how genetic uniformity doomed the Gros Michel; the last sentence notes the Cavendish is just as dominant and is now under attack, implying history may repeat.

B.rationale: The reason for choosing the Cavendish (its resistance) appears in the previous sentence.

C.rationale: The last sentence describes a new threat, not a solution.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests the Gros Michel has returned.

hints: What does "in the same way" connect?

strategy.explanation: Compare the last sentence with the history before it.

candidates.remember: A closing sentence often links a past case to a present one.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: switched to the swarming form even faster than untreated locusts.
choices.B: began producing more serotonin than locusts that were not crowded.
choices.C: largely failed to switch to the swarming form.
choices.D: stopped responding to touch on any part of their bodies.

candidates.evidence: was accompanied by a sharp rise in serotonin
candidates.explanation: If the rise in serotonin is what drives the switch, blocking serotonin should prevent crowded locusts from switching.

A.rationale: If serotonin drives the switch, blocking it should slow or prevent the switch, not speed it up.

B.rationale: The drug blocks serotonin's effects; nothing suggests it increases production.

D.rationale: The text concerns the switch to swarming, not a general loss of touch sensation.

hints: What role does serotonin seem to play?

strategy.explanation: Predict the result of removing the key factor.

candidates.remember: When a factor is blocked, predict the effect it was causing to disappear.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researchers' conclusion?

choices.A: Light-tolerant bats made 55 passes under red light and 90 under white light.
choices.B: Light-avoiding bats made 40 passes in darkness, compared with 50 for light-tolerant bats.
choices.C: Light-avoiding bats made 36 passes under red light, compared with 55 for light-tolerant bats.
choices.D: Light-avoiding bats made 36 passes under red light and 40 in darkness but only 10 under white light.

candidates.evidence: red light let light-avoiding bats remain nearly as active as they were in darkness, unlike white light
candidates.explanation: The conclusion compares three conditions for light-avoiding bats; D gives all three: 36 (red), 40 (dark), 10 (white).

A.rationale: This concerns the other group of bats, not the light-avoiding species the conclusion is about.

B.rationale: This compares the two groups in darkness and says nothing about red or white light.

C.rationale: This compares the two groups under red light but not red light with darkness or white light.

hints: Which group and which conditions does the conclusion name?

strategy.explanation: Match every condition in the claim to the table.

candidates.remember: Check the right column before checking the numbers.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the critics in Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion described in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that language shapes thought, since the Guugu Yimithirr speakers performed well on direction tests even indoors
choices.B: By suggesting that environment and daily habits, rather than language alone, may explain the speakers' strong sense of direction
choices.C: By arguing that Guugu Yimithirr speakers do not actually keep track of compass directions as accurately as reported
choices.D: By claiming that the environment people live in has no real effect on how they think about space and direction

candidates.evidence: sense of direction tracked environment and habits about as closely as it tracked language
candidates.explanation: Text 2 offers a competing explanation: environment and habits, which often accompany such languages, may account for the skill.

A.rationale: The critics question whether language is the cause; they do not simply agree.

C.rationale: Text 2 does not dispute the speakers' accuracy, only its cause.

D.rationale: Text 2 argues the opposite: environment tracked sense of direction closely.

hints: What alternative cause does Text 2 propose?

strategy.explanation: Identify the claim, then the challenge to it.

candidates.remember: A confounding factor challenges a causal claim without denying the observation.

candidates.stem: The student wants to contrast the kinds of light the two telescopes observe. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: While Hubble observes mainly visible and ultraviolet light, Webb observes mainly infrared light, which can pass through dust.
choices.B: Hubble was launched in 1990, more than thirty years before the Webb telescope was launched in 2021.
choices.C: Webb orbits about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth, which is much farther away than Hubble's orbit.
choices.D: Launched in 2021, Webb observes mainly infrared light, which can pass through the clouds of dust that block visible light.

candidates.evidence: Hubble observes mainly visible and ultraviolet light.
candidates.explanation: The goal is to contrast the light each telescope observes; A names both and sets them against each other.

B.rationale: This contrasts launch dates, not the kinds of light observed.

C.rationale: This contrasts locations, not the kinds of light observed.

D.rationale: This describes only Webb and does not contrast it with Hubble.

hints: Which choice names the light for both telescopes?

strategy.explanation: Check that the choice compares both items on the named feature.

candidates.remember: A contrast must mention both items and the specific difference named in the goal.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: In trials, however, it prevented about 95 percent of cases
candidates.explanation: The text first concedes a drawback and then, with "however," turns to the vaccine's strength. "Granted" introduces a concession at the start.

A.rationale: The cold-storage requirement is not a result of anything stated before it.

B.rationale: Nothing earlier is being made more specific.

D.rationale: There is no earlier statement for this one to resemble.

hints: Is the first sentence a drawback that the writer will answer?
candidates.remember: "Granted" concedes a point the writer will then counter.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: where do European eels go to spawn
candidates.explanation: The words after the colon form a direct question with inverted word order, so the sentence ends with a question mark.

A.rationale: "Where do European eels go to spawn" is a direct question (note the inverted "do eels go"), so it needs a question mark.

C.rationale: The sentence asks a question; an exclamation point does not fit.

D.rationale: A semicolon would join the question to the next sentence, which begins with a capital letter and stands alone.

hints: Is the part after the colon asked directly?

strategy.explanation: Look for inverted question word order.

candidates.remember: A direct question ends with a question mark even after a colon.

candidates.subskill: Verb tense in a past counterfactual
candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: the heat would probably have broken it apart
candidates.explanation: For an unreal past condition paired with "would have broken," the "if" clause uses the past perfect: "if the comet had passed."

A.rationale: "Would" belongs in the result clause; the "if" clause of a past counterfactual takes "had" + past participle.

B.rationale: The present tense does not fit a hypothetical event in 2020.

C.rationale: The present perfect does not fit an unreal condition in the past.

hints: Did the comet actually pass that close?
candidates.remember: Past unreal: if + had + past participle, ... would have + past participle.
